title: Encode/Decode Strings
description: Serialize a list of arbitrary strings into one string and round-trip it back. Length-prefix scheme `len#payload` avoids any delimiter collision.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: I need two functions — `encode(strs)` that takes a list of arbitrary strings and produces a single string, and `decode(str)` that takes that string back to the original list. The round trip must be lossless for any input. A few critical clarifying questions:"

• What's the character domain of the input strings — ASCII, full Unicode, or arbitrary bytes? This decides what we can use as a delimiter.
• Can the strings be empty? Can the input list be empty?
• Is the encoded form constrained — must it be ASCII-printable, or anything goes?
• Am I optimizing for encode/decode speed, or for the smallest encoded size?
sections.why: The character-domain question is the most important one in this whole problem. If the answer is 'arbitrary strings including any Unicode codepoint,' then no single character can serve as a safe delimiter — payloads might contain it. That's the entire motivation for the length-prefix scheme. Confirming it up front turns the rest of the conversation into 'here's why length-prefix is the right answer' rather than 'why didn't you just join with a comma?'

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the naive solution and walk through why it breaks.
sections.say:
"The naive solution is to pick a separator and `join` on it — `strs.join('#')`. Decode would be `str.split('#')`. That works perfectly UNTIL the input contains the separator: `encode(['a', '#b'])` produces `'a##b'`, and `'a##b'.split('#')` gives `['a', '', 'b']` — three elements, not two. The round trip is broken."

"You could try escaping — replace `'#'` in payloads with `'\\#'` and unescape on decode — but now you've got escape rules to track, and you have to escape the escape character too. It's brittle."

"The clean fix is to make the encoding self-describing: instead of relying on a delimiter to find the boundary, prefix each payload with its length. Then the decoder doesn't need to scan for a delimiter inside the payload at all — it reads the length, jumps that far, and lands on the next header."
sections.why: This is the unusual case where the brute force ISN'T O(n²) — it's the wrong solution, period. Walking through how `split('#')` breaks with a concrete payload (`'#b'`) is the move that earns the length-prefix solution. Saying 'I'd use a length prefix' without first showing why simpler approaches fail is just memorization.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to length-prefix framing?
sections.say:
"This is a self-delimiting encoding problem — the structural property is that the encoded form must be unambiguously parseable without external context, and the payload alphabet overlaps with any candidate delimiter alphabet. The classic solution: encode each item as `length` + `delimiter` + `payload`. The length tells the decoder exactly how many bytes to consume for the payload, so the delimiter only needs to separate the length-header from the payload — and the length is digits, which can't collide with the `'#'` separator."

"This is the same trick that powers Pascal strings, network protocols like HTTP's `Content-Length`, and serialization formats like Protobuf and BSON. Length-prefix beats delimiter-scan whenever payloads can be arbitrary."
sections.why: Naming the encoding pattern AND the structural property — 'self-delimiting framing where payload alphabet overlaps delimiter alphabet' — is what separates this from a memorized template. The comparison to HTTP `Content-Length` and Protobuf is the senior-tier touch: it shows you've seen this problem in production, not just on a problem set.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace a couple of round trips." Three cases — a typical two-string input, an empty string in the list (the case that breaks naive delimiter schemes), and a payload containing the delimiter character itself (the case that proves length-prefix earns its keep).

examples.trace:
ENCODE:
s="hello" (len 5) → out += "5#hello" → out="5#hello"
s="world" (len 5) → out += "5#world" → out="5#hello5#world"
DECODE str="5#hello5#world":
i=0: scan to '#' at j=1. len=Number("5")=5. payload=str.slice(2,7)="hello". push. i=j+1+len=1+1+5=7
i=7: scan to '#' at j=8. len=Number("5")=5. payload=str.slice(9,14)="world". push. i=8+1+5=14
return ["hello","world"] ✓

examples.note: Empty string — encodes as `0#`, decodes back to `[""]`. Naive `split(',')` could lose this case entirely.
examples.trace:
ENCODE:
s="" (len 0) → out += "0#" → out="0#"
DECODE str="0#":
i=0: scan to '#' at j=1. len=Number("0")=0. payload=str.slice(2,2)="". push. i=1+1+0=2
loop ends (i=2=str.length)
return [""] ✓

examples.note: Payload contains '#' itself — this is the case that proves length-prefix beats delimiter-scan. Notice we never try to interpret the '#' inside `#b` as a delimiter.
examples.trace:
ENCODE:
s="a" (len 1) → out="1#a"
s="#b" (len 2) → out="1#a2##b"
s="c" (len 1) → out="1#a2##b1#c"
DECODE str="1#a2##b1#c":
i=0: scan to '#' at j=1. len=1. payload=str.slice(2,3)="a". push. i=3
i=3: scan to '#' at j=4. len=2. payload=str.slice(5,7)="#b". push. i=7  ← length-prefix consumed the '#' as payload, NOT delimiter
i=7: scan to '#' at j=8. len=1. payload=str.slice(9,10)="c". push. i=10
return ["a","#b","c"] ✓

sections.why: The third example is the one to mention out loud — it's the case that justifies the entire design. The trace shows the decoder NEVER mistakes the `'#'` inside `'#b'` for a delimiter, because once it's read length=2 it just consumes 2 chars of payload mechanically. The empty-string case is also worth narrating; many candidates' first instinct is to filter empties out, which breaks lossless round-tripping.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges worth flagging:"

• Empty list `[]` → encodes to `""`, decodes back to `[]` (the while loop never enters).
• List with empty strings (`[""]`, `["", ""]`) → encodes as `0#`, `0#0#`. Length-prefix handles them cleanly.
• Payload containing `'#'` → handled because we scan to the FIRST `'#'` per header, not any `'#'`.
• Payload containing digits at the front → no problem, because the digits BEFORE the first `'#'` are unambiguously the header.
• Very long payload → string concatenation in encode is technically O(n²) on some engines; for production you'd use an array + join at the end. Not usually an issue in practice for V8.
• Unicode/emoji → `s.length` returns UTF-16 code units, not codepoints. A single emoji counts as length 2. As long as encode and decode both use `.length` and `.slice`, the round trip is still correct — both sides agree on the unit. But if someone consumes the encoded form by codepoint count, they'd be off.
sections.why: The Unicode call-out is the senior-tier touch — `.length` and `.slice` are consistent (both UTF-16 units) so the round trip is correct internally, but the encoded form is undefined behavior if a *different* system tries to parse it counting codepoints. That kind of cross-system reasoning is what separates implementations from production code. The O(n²) string-concat note also shows depth — knowing that the canonical might not be optimal at scale.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(N) where N is the total character count across all input strings. Encode does one pass with O(1) per char (modulo string-concat caveats above). Decode does one pass with O(1) per char — the inner while that scans for `'#'` looks like it could be O(k²), but each character is visited at most twice (once by the scan, once by the slice), so the amortized cost is O(N) total.

Space is O(N) — the encoded string and the decoded list both hold the same total character payload.

If you wanted to extend this: the same length-prefix framing scales to nested structures (encode a list of lists by recursively prefixing). For binary data, you'd swap the digit-header for a fixed-width 4-byte big-endian length, which is what most network protocols actually do. Same template — self-delimiting via explicit length — at every scale."
sections.why: The amortization defense for the decode's nested while loop is the move — without it, an interviewer might press you on 'isn't that nested?' The recursive-nested and binary-protocol extensions show you see this as a *template*, which is the truth: every serialization format in production uses some flavor of length-prefix or escape-and-delimit, and length-prefix wins for anything where the payload alphabet isn't restricted. That's the senior-track wrap-up.

notes: Length-prefix is delimiter-safe: payloads can contain '#' or any character.
Find '#' via a scan, not split — the payload may itself contain '#'.
Empty string encodes as `0#`; empty array encodes as `""` and decodes to `[]`.

questions.q: Why prefix with `length + '#'` instead of just joining on a separator?
options: Any separator could collide with a payload character — length prefix is collision-proof

questions.q: When decoding, why scan for '#' instead of using `split('#')`?
options: Payloads themselves can contain '#', so a global split would over-split

questions.q: How is the empty string `""` encoded?
After reading length L from a header ending at index j, where does the next header begin?
questions.explain: Skip the '#' (1 char) and the payload (L chars).

questions.q: Why can the digit characters of the length header never be confused with the payload that follows?
options: The first '#' marks the boundary — everything before it is the header, everything after (for `len` chars) is payload
questions.explain: The decoder scans to the FIRST '#' to read the length, then consumes exactly `len` chars — the header digits and payload are separated by that boundary, not by ambiguity.

questions.q: Why does the naive `strs.join('#')` then `split('#')` round trip break?
options: If a payload itself contains '#', split produces extra pieces and the count no longer matches
questions.explain: A delimiter that can also appear inside a payload is ambiguous — `['a','#b']` joins to `'a##b'` and splits to three pieces, losing the original boundaries.

questions.q: How does the empty array [] round-trip?
options: Encodes to '0' then errors on decode
Encodes to '' and decodes back to [] because the while loop never enters
questions.explain: No strings means nothing is concatenated, so encode returns '', and decode's `while (i < str.length)` is immediately false, yielding [].

questions.q: Length-prefix framing is robust precisely when:
options: The payload alphabet can overlap any candidate delimiter, so no separator char is reserved-safe
All strings are the same length
questions.explain: When payloads may contain arbitrary characters, no single delimiter is safe; encoding an explicit length makes the framing self-describing regardless of payload contents.

L3.prompt: Implement `encode(strs)` and `decode(str)` using a length-prefix scheme. Log `encode(["hello","world"])` then `JSON.stringify(decode(encode(["hello","world"])))`.
hints: Encode each string as `length + '#' + payload` and concatenate.
To decode, scan to '#', read the length, slice off that many chars.
